presentingComplaint: Two weeks of increasing lethargy, poor appetite and breathlessness, with new fast irregular heartbeat; brought in confused and mildly jaundiced.
history: Elderly widow living alone, brought by her daughter for 2 weeks of uncharacteristic apathy, low mood and withdrawal rather than agitation. Progressive fatigue, anorexia and 6 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 months. Loose stools 3-4 times daily for a week and intermittent nausea. Daughter reports new palpitations and ankle swelling. No classic heat intolerance, sweating or tremor volunteered. Background of long-standing nodular goitre that was never investigated; recently started amiodarone by a peripheral clinic for palpitations 6 weeks ago (likely precipitant). No sedative or antipsychotic exposure, no serotonergic drugs, no fever-inducing illness identified. On presentation she is drowsy and disoriented to time and place.
examination: Frail, apathetic elderly woman, minimally interactive (apathetic thyrotoxicosis phenotype). Warm peripheries, fine skin. Small firm multinodular goitre palpable, no bruit appreciated over noise. No exophthalmos or lid lag. Irregularly irregular pulse ~140/min with pulse deficit. Raised JVP, bibasal crepitations and bilateral pitting pedal oedema (high-output failure). Mild scleral icterus, tender smooth hepatomegaly. Fine distal tremor when hands examined. Drowsy, GCS 13 (E3V4M6), no focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness. Reflexes brisk.

labs.bwScore: Burch-Wartofsky 60 (temp 15 + CNS 20 + GI/hepatic 10 + tachycardia 15 + CHF 10, minus precipitant absent) — highly suggestive of thyroid storm

imaging: ECG: atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response ~140/min, no acute ischaemia. Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly with mild upper-lobe diversion and small bilateral effusions consistent with congestive failure. Bedside echo: preserved-to-hyperdynamic LV, no tamponade.
microbiology: Blood cultures and urine culture sent to exclude sepsis as mimic/precipitant; no source identified. Not infective.
differentialDiagnoses: Rapid atrial fibrillation with rate-related decompensation
finalDiagnosis: Thyroid storm (apathetic, cardiac-predominant variant) precipitated by amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis on a background nodular goitre; Burch-Wartofsky score 60.
citations: American Thyroid Association (ATA) — Hyperthyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis, 2016
Burch & Wartofsky — Diagnostic Criteria for Thyroid Storm, 1993
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Thyroid Gland / Thyrotoxic Crisis
stewardship: Non-infective endocrine emergency; no empiric antibiotics indicated. Send cultures to exclude an occult precipitant but do not start antimicrobials without a source.
contraindications: Avoid abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal and use cautiously given congestive failure; use rate control with monitoring
Do NOT give iodine (Lugol's/SSKI) until at least 1 hour after thionamide to avoid substrate for hormone synthesis
Salicylates contraindicated for pyrexia (displace T4 from binding proteins, worsen thyrotoxicosis) — use paracetamol
Amiodarone must be stopped (precipitant); avoid further iodinated contrast
edgeCases: Apathetic presentation in the elderly can be mistaken for depression, dementia or sepsis, delaying diagnosis
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (type 1 vs 2) may need combined thionamide plus glucocorticoid
Absence of high fever or florid agitation does not exclude storm — Burch-Wartofsky remains high
Congestive hepatopathy causing jaundice can be misread as primary liver disease
expectedMaiK: Recognise decompensated thyrotoxicosis (thyroid storm) despite the atypical apathetic presentation using the Burch-Wartofsky score, and begin multimodal therapy: beta-blockade (rate control), a thionamide (propylthiouracil/carbimazole), iodine given >1h after thionamide, and stress-dose hydrocortisone, while stopping amiodarone and supporting heart failure.
expectedNextQuestions: Any recent iodinated contrast, amiodarone, or antithyroid drug cessation as a precipitant?
History of goitre, prior thyroid disease or radio-iodine?
Any concurrent infection, surgery or trauma?
Baseline cognition and functional status (to interpret the apathy/confusion)?
expectedInvestigations: TSH, free T4 and free T3
Liver function tests and coagulation profile
Blood and urine cultures to screen for a precipitating infection
Serum calcium, glucose, renal profile and electrolytes
regressionAssertions: Engine must rank thyroid_storm as the top diagnosis despite absence of florid agitation/heat intolerance
Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3 plus high Burch-Wartofsky must drive the endocrine emergency over primary AF or heart failure
No empiric antibiotics should be recommended (non-infective); cultures only to exclude precipitant
Iodine must be sequenced after thionamide, and salicylate antipyretics must be flagged as contraindicated
